title: Network Optimization II: Flows, Paths & Supply Chain Design
subtitle: Shortest paths, max flow, and min-cost flow — the models behind Amazon's regionalized network and Microsoft's Edelman-winning fulfillment engine

objectives.title: Formulate the three classic flow models
objectives.description: Write shortest path, maximum flow, and minimum-cost flow problems as linear programs on a network, and recognize which real business questions map to each.

objectives.title: Design a supply chain network end to end
objectives.description: Combine facility choices, arc capacities, and transportation costs into a single network design model that decides where product flows and why.

objectives.title: Connect flow models to billion-dollar operations
objectives.description: Explain how Amazon's regionalization and Microsoft's Intelligent Fulfillment Service turned textbook network optimization into measurable cost-to-serve and cycle-time wins.

objectives.title: Build and solve networks in gurobipy
objectives.description: Implement node-balance constraints, capacity bounds, and flow costs cleanly in code, and read the solution as a routing plan a logistics manager could execute.

agenda.title: Opening Story: Amazon Regionalizes, Microsoft Wins the Edelman
agenda.description: Two of the biggest supply chain analytics stories of the decade — and both are network flow problems at heart.
bulletPoints: Amazon 'Regionalize and Scale' (2025 Edelman finalist): splitting the US into regional networks cut cost-to-serve by $0.45 per item in 2023
Microsoft Intelligent Fulfillment Service (2026 Edelman WINNER): cloud hardware fulfillment cycle times cut in half, tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in annual savings
The common thread: nodes, arcs, capacities, and costs — the same math you will write tonight

agenda.title: Shortest Path & Max Flow
agenda.description: The two foundational flow models, formulated as LPs and interpreted as business questions.
bulletPoints: Shortest path: cheapest route from source to sink — one unit of flow, minimize arc costs
Max flow: how much can this network carry? Capacities become the binding constraints
Bottleneck reading: the max-flow / min-cut insight tells you exactly where to invest capacity

agenda.title: Min-Cost Flow: The Workhorse Model
agenda.description: One formulation that generalizes almost everything: supplies, demands, capacities, and per-unit costs on a single network.
bulletPoints: Node balance constraints: flow in minus flow out equals supply or demand
Transportation, transshipment, and assignment as special cases of min-cost flow
Integrality for free: why network LPs return whole-number flows without integer variables

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch, refill, and think about where the bottleneck arc in your own company's network might be.

agenda.title: Hands-On: DC Location + Routing in gurobipy
agenda.description: In teams, build a mini supply chain network design model: pick distribution centers and route flow from plants to customer regions at minimum total cost.
bulletPoints: Define plants, candidate DCs, and demand regions as nodes; lanes as capacitated arcs
Add flow variables, node-balance constraints, and lane capacities in gurobipy
Solve, then stress-test: what happens when a lane's capacity drops 40%?

agenda.title: Supply Chain Network Design at Scale
agenda.description: From tonight's toy network to Amazon-scale: what changes, what doesn't, and how practitioners handle it.
bulletPoints: Regionalization as a network design decision: shorter arcs, higher in-region fulfillment rates
Microsoft's IFS pattern: optimization embedded in daily operations, not a one-off study
Scaling levers: aggregation, decomposition, and GPU-accelerated solvers like NVIDIA cuOpt

agenda.title: Wrap-Up & Homework #4 Launch
agenda.description: Key takeaways, a preview of integer optimization, and your min-cost flow assignment.
bulletPoints: Recap: three flow models, one node-balance idea
Homework #4 walkthrough: a min-cost flow model from scratch
Next week: when yes/no decisions enter the model, everything changes

activities.title: Mini Network Design: Pick the DCs, Route the Flow
activities.description: Your team is the supply chain analytics group for a mid-size retailer. Two plants, three candidate distribution centers, four demand regions. Build a min-cost flow model in gurobipy that routes product through the network and reveals which DC lanes carry the load.

steps.title: Sketch the network
steps.description: Draw nodes for plants, DCs, and regions. Label supplies, demands, lane costs, and capacities before writing any code — the picture is the formulation.

steps.title: Code the flow variables and balance constraints
steps.description: One continuous variable per arc; at every DC, flow in must equal flow out; plants ship at most their supply, regions receive exactly their demand.

steps.title: Solve and interpret
steps.description: Run the model, then translate the solution into plain English: which lanes are used, which DC dominates, and what the marginal cost of one more unit of regional demand is.

steps.title: Stress-test the network
steps.description: Cut one lane's capacity by 40% and re-solve. How does the flow re-route, and what does total cost do? This is regionalization analysis in miniature.

codeBlock.code:
import gurobipy as gp
from gurobipy import GRB

plants = {"P1": 500, "P2": 400}          # supply
regions = {"R1": 200, "R2": 250, "R3": 180, "R4": 220}  # demand
dcs = ["DC_A", "DC_B", "DC_C"]

# (from, to): (unit cost, capacity)
lanes = {
    ("P1", "DC_A"): (4, 400), ("P1", "DC_B"): (6, 300),
    ("P2", "DC_B"): (5, 350), ("P2", "DC_C"): (4, 300),
    ("DC_A", "R1"): (3, 250), ("DC_A", "R2"): (5, 250),
    ("DC_B", "R2"): (4, 300), ("DC_B", "R3"): (3, 250),
    ("DC_C", "R3"): (5, 200), ("DC_C", "R4"): (2, 250),
}

m = gp.Model("network_design")
flow = m.addVars(lanes.keys(), name="flow",
                 ub=[lanes[a][1] for a in lanes])

m.setObjective(gp.quicksum(lanes[a][0] * flow[a] for a in lanes), GRB.MINIMIZE)

for p, s in plants.items():
    m.addConstr(flow.sum(p, "*") <= s, name=f"supply_{p}")
for d in dcs:
    m.addConstr(flow.sum("*", d) == flow.sum(d, "*"), name=f"balance_{d}")
for r, dem in regions.items():
    m.addConstr(flow.sum("*", r) == dem, name=f"demand_{r}")

m.optimize()
for a in lanes:
    if flow[a].X > 1e-6:
        print(f"{a[0]} -> {a[1]}: {flow[a].X:.0f} units")
print(f"Total cost: ${m.ObjVal:,.0f}")

activities.discussionNote: Amazon's regionalization win came from exactly this logic at continental scale: shorten the arcs between inventory and customers and the cost-to-serve falls — $0.45 per item across billions of items. Where in your team's solution did flow travel 'too far,' and what candidate node would you add to fix it?

takeaways.text: Shortest path, max flow, and min-cost flow are one family: node-balance constraints plus arc capacities. Master the min-cost flow template and you can model most physical supply chains.

This math wins at the highest level — Amazon's regionalization cut US cost-to-serve $0.45/item, and Microsoft's Intelligent Fulfillment Service won the 2026 Edelman by halving fulfillment cycle times.
The solution is only half the value. Which lanes bind, where the min cut sits, and how flow re-routes under stress — that is the analysis executives actually pay for.
